title: Critics Hammond and Spike Hughes on his sophistication
summary: Brown understands why critics thought his sweet concert style out of place and compares it to Paul Whiteman's symphonic jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Again, in Barry Ulanov's book, he mentioned that John Hammond wrote about you saying after he first heard you with Duke, "He's a virtuoso of the first rank, one who is very conscious of his technical ability. Probably no other trombonist has his equipment, but I'm afraid that this brilliant musician is out of place in Duke's band." And then there's some quotes from Spike Hughes (of The Melody Maker) who felt that you were too sophisticated for jazz and Duke Ellington. Do you remember that?

Well, I -- I can see what they would mean because the era before me -- well, colored bands didn't play sophisticated music. They were jazz bands. You know, the old tail gate type or roughous type of music. Very few of them

played real sweet. And since that was my type of music, why that's all I knew. In fact, that's all I was going to play because I -- for the first years when I was out on the road, I had California in my eye, and I was going back at the drop of a hat. In fact, I left my car on blocks the whole time I was on the road for about 20 years and -- because I didn't care anything about the road, you know. I would go home in a minutes. So, I can see where they thought that was (unintelligible).

In fact, I would liken that to the situation with Paul Whiteman. When Paul Whiteman first brought out his syncosymphony, that was the first time they had ever joined -- had a marriage between two types of music. So, it was the same thing.

So, it was the same thing. Here's this colored jazz playing something sweet, or something concertish, or something like that. I could see where they would resent it because it was new. People resent anything new, see, until they become conscious of it and they think it's great.
Do you think that was maybe around the time Duke began resenting being identified with jazz, or being tied down to what he considered the limitations of the definition of jazz? No?
Well, I don't know. I think those things spring from inner desires to get away from the old staid atmospheres that they are categorized with. And I think
that's a the case of that because we still had to retain much, much of that jungle type band. And I think that -- well, these things are just a case of progress -- the change to fit the progress.
How did Duke feel about John Hammond and Spike Hughes.
I don't know. I never -- I never did much association with too many of the rest of the people.
